chunks: "I think in layers, starting where the interference enters.

At the connector, every line that leaves the board gets protection and filtering right at the connector: a TVS or ESD diode with a short, wide return to chassis or ground for transients, a ferrite bead or common-mode choke for RF, and a small capacitor.
Putting it there matters, because anything between the connector and the filter gets the full noise. Second, I make the victim hard to disturb.
Sensitive analog inputs get an RC low-pass right at the amplifier pins, with low and balanced source impedance, because RF will rectify in input junctions otherwise.
I keep high-impedance nodes short and put guard or ground around them, use differential signalling for anything long, and use a solid ground plane so the loops are small and returns are controlled.

Third, partition the board so sensitive circuitry is away from the connectors and noisy sections, and bond connector shells to chassis with low inductance so ESD current goes around the logic, not through it.
And in firmware and reset circuits, add robustness: filtered resets, watchdog, brown-out, retry and checksums. Shield cans and enclosure shielding come last."
